top_comments: These are Ghostty GUI release notes, but I want to take a moment to highlight the libghostty progress we've made since Ghostty 1.3.As a reminder, libghostty is the highly portable, embeddable library that provides core terminal emulation, render state, and more. I always felt that a free, high qualty, lightweight, reusable terminal emulation core would benefit the developer world more than any single GUI application. And that is playing out!It is and always was my true purpose with the Ghostty project (I said this in my first ever talk about Ghostty!). I've jokingly said many times that Ghostty GUI is just a glorified tech demo for libghostty. That's not fair though, because GUI is great and there are really talented people working on it.Since I started the project, Ghostty has always gotten people saying "I don't understand why you'd start a terminal emulator today." Well, the answer is libghostty. It's truly unique and its enabling something special (imo!).Highlights of libghostty since 6 months ago (none of the below was true 6 months ago):- Libghostty has nearly 100% coverage of all of Ghostty's core (and you can compile with flags to remove any of these features for size/safety): https://libghostty.tip.ghostty.org/- Libghostty now builds and is tested (in CI) for: Apple (macOS, iOS, visionOS), Windows (MSVC and GNU), Linux, FreeBSD, Android, WebAssembly, and freestanding (i.e. direct on hardware with no OS).- Libghostty has bindings in pretty much every popular programming language: C, Zig, Go, Swift, Python, Rust, .NET, etc.- Libghostty's memory requirements have dramatically shrunk to enable the portability above. There's still work to do but a single empty terminal now takes 90% less memory. And at scale I've proven 10,000 active (input/output happening) terminals on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM.- Libghostty powers all JetBrains IDE terminals, over 12.5 million active users. https://blog.jetbrains.com/platform/2026/10/jetbrains-termin...- Libghostty is the most popular core behind the wave of venture-backed "agentic" terminals and editors, such as Herdr, cmux, and many others.- Libghostty is being discussed and has been verbally accepted to replace the terminal core in Neovim: https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/39773 (work still to be done)- Libghostty powers a really popular and powerful terminal emulator for emacs (Ghostel): https://github.com/dakra/ghostel- Libghostty's speed is used by Antithesis to fuzz popular terminal programs and has directly led to hundreds of bug fixes sent upstream to programs such as tmux, btop, shells, and other terminal emulators. :)- And so much more: https://github.com/Uzaaft/awesome-libghosttyLibghostty is really successfully turning into the tide that raises all boats. As it becomes more popular, Ghostty itself gets more performant and stable, and so does everyone else. It is also a vehicle for delivering modern terminal emulation to the widest source possible.I plan on tagging libghostty 1.0 in the next few months and declaring ABI stability at that point!

I've tried Ghostty and it's great, but Kitty's hints mode[1] is the one feature keeping me from switching from Kitty to Ghostty. There are quite a few discussions around this and similar features in the Ghosstty-org/ghostty Discussions[2] which I follow. Most of them are references from ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/2394[3]. Maybe now that Ghostty has finished implementing Kitty graphics hints will be next .[1]: https://sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/kittens/hints/[2]: https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions[3]: https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/2394

I still don't understand the point of Ghostty, Kitty, Wezterm...Konsole is way faster than any of those on my computer and it has all the usual suspects I'd expect from a modern terminal emulator.The one feature I miss since moving to Linux and not having iTerm2 is tmux -CC integration. None of those offer it.To be clear, I'm not attempting to be dismissive. I really want to understand what it is that they bring.

articles.title: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update
articles.summary: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update

top_comments: Former tailscalar here and now someone managing tailscale at an org.Having done my own review of the vulns and the fixes as they are landing in github, its pretty clear to me that this only affects situations where you use ACLs to permit ssh into a node (via tailscale ssh, not via opensshd), but dont give a path to sudoers/root.If a user had no SSH access and/or connectivity to a vulnerable node, none of these vulns give them access.However, if you have a vulnerable tailscaled and you give ssh access as some non-root account/privs, then yes, these vulns are relevant as theres now known privilege escalations that give access beyond some specific user account.Not trying to play down the vuln (its important), but its not a free-for-all RCE that some ppl are acting like it is.

I am fairly glad I have stuck with stock OpenSSH that ships with Linux. This incident proves I am glad with that choice.Over the decades, I have maintained remote access through port forwarding on my router - at one point in 2008 I put SSH on port 80 so I could access it from the restricted wifi network at the hospital my grandmother was at. I have also used openvpn. I have also used cloudflare tunnels. But in the end, I always connect to hardened openssh with key only authentication.

Somehow I don't think it's a good idea to let Tailscale handle service authentication at all. It's supposed to be an additional security layer around existing infrastructure and services.Letting Tailscale handle VPN and SSH at the same time is basically once again a single point of failure. Similar to exposing SSH directly to the internet.

articles.title: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer
articles.summary: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer

top_comments: This topic is bringing out the hallucination-panic crowd.It's perfectly safe to use LLMs to surface underlying data and knowledge without having to trust that it's giving you correct advice.Use the LLM as search technology: string match -> semantic search -> search intelligence.This is especially helpful when you don't know the right question to ask. Semantics only help you find text that is semantically near the input query. Semantics won't help you when what you are looking for is connected to what you have by something other than semantics, like causation, mechanism, or interpretation.Trying to figure out why your crops aren't growing well will likely require you to read several articles across a range of sciences, probably scoped to the specific conditions you are dealing with. A semantic search is not going to surface those first.Allowing an LLM to chain together several sources for you to read first does not require you to ask it for a conclusion.

I set this up on my machine and tested it with the following question:How can I build a bow drill so I can start a fire?It got it partially right: spindle, bow with string tied the correct way, and fire board. But then it flubbed by saying you put the spindle between both hands and move your hands back and forth to rotate the spindle and create the necessary friction… this totally ignores using the bow to rotate the spindle! It also mentioned “fanning the sparks” but there is absolutely no way your bow drill is going to create sparks.I asked a frontier model to check the survival LLM’s conversation trace and it pointed out the errors.I didn’t see obvious errors in the other 3 prompts I used, but this one seemed pretty egregious for a survival LLM.I thank the creator for making this, but take it with a grain of salt.
Shoutout to project nomad.https://www.projectnomad.us/its got a ton of useful options, preconfigured, integrates pretty easily, and can use any local LLM or data.

articles.title: Classification of Finite Simple Groups Formalized in Lean
articles.summary: Classification of Finite Simple Groups Formalized in Lean

top_comments: Out of curiosity: is it possible to take a frontier model and just let it loose on all math textbooks out there, converting each and every proof/theorem/lemma/etc. into Lean? A frontier model should be able to do that, right? And it's a one-time task: do it once and it's there for eternity, available as a library to be used in other proofs.Maybe my understanding of Lean is wrong; I'm thinking of it as a programming language but for Math.

This seems like a very good use of auto-formalization, because in the past mathematicians have incorrectly believed that they were finished with the classification only discover a missing class/sporadic group.The original proof was a collaboration of ~100 mathematicians, if Tao is correct then we should expect to see more such collaborations in the future like we do in e.g. physics.
Makes me sad that the homotopical foundation people never got their shit together and now formalization is so mature but it's still done in set theoretic foundations.
